back: Vacuum tube: bulky, high power, works at about 100 V, short life, needs a heated cathode and an evacuated space, current flows only cathode to anode (hence 'valve'). Semiconductor device: small, low power, low voltage, long life, high reliability, carriers supplied and moved inside the solid itself.

Metals: very low resistivity, about 10^-8 to 10^-2 ohm m. Semiconductors: intermediate, about 10^-5 to 10^6 ohm m. Insulators: very high resistivity, about 10^11 to 10^19 ohm m. Resistivity alone is not the only criterion.

front: Valence band, conduction band, energy gap
back: Valence band: the band containing the energy levels of the valence electrons. Conduction band: the band above it. Energy band gap E_g: the gap between the top of the valence band (E_V) and the bottom of the conduction band (E_C).

front: Band picture of metal, insulator and semiconductor
back: Metal: conduction band partly filled or overlapping the valence band, gap about zero. Insulator: valence band full, conduction band empty, E_g > 3 eV. Semiconductor: valence band full, conduction band nearly empty, E_g < 3 eV.

A pure semiconductor with no added impurity. Carriers exist only because thermal energy breaks covalent bonds, so electrons and holes are created in equal numbers and the conductivity is very low at room temperature.

front: Covalent bonding in Si and Ge
back: Both crystallise in diamond-like structures. Each atom shares one of its four valence electrons with each of four neighbours, and the shared pair (a covalent or valence bond) shuttles between the atoms and holds them together strongly.

The vacancy left in a bond when a valence electron breaks free. It carries effective charge +q and behaves as an apparent free particle with effective positive charge; a neighbouring bound electron filling it makes the hole appear to move.
n_e = n_h = n_i  ... Eq. (14.1). n_i is the intrinsic carrier concentration: equal numbers of free electrons and holes in a pure semiconductor.
I = I_e + I_h  ... Eq. (14.2). Both electrons and holes carry current: holes drift towards the negative potential while electrons give the electron current.
Thermal energy generates electron-hole pairs; simultaneously electrons recombine with holes on collision. At equilibrium the generation rate equals the recombination rate, which fixes n_i.

Deliberate addition of a few ppm of a suitable impurity (dopant) to a pure semiconductor increases its conductivity manifold. The resulting material is an extrinsic (impurity, doped) semiconductor. The dopant must fit the lattice, so it is taken from group V or group III.

As, Sb or P in a Si/Ge lattice: four electrons bond with the neighbours and the fifth is very weakly bound. Only about 0.01 eV (Ge) or 0.05 eV (Si) frees it, against 0.72 eV / 1.1 eV to cross the whole gap. One donor gives one electron, so the material is n-type.

In, B or Al has one valence electron less, so it forms only three bonds and leaves a hole in the fourth. The trivalent core becomes negatively charged on taking a fourth electron. One acceptor gives one hole, so the material is p-type.

Doped with a pentavalent donor. Electrons are the majority carriers, holes the minority carriers: n_e >> n_h  ... Eq. (14.3). Total electrons = donated + intrinsic; holes come only from intrinsic generation, further reduced by recombination. The crystal stays neutral.

Doped with a trivalent acceptor. Holes are the majority carriers, electrons the minority carriers: n_h >> n_e  ... Eq. (14.4). Conduction electrons come only from intrinsic generation; the crystal stays neutral because the ionised cores balance the extra holes.
n_e n_h = n_i^2  ... Eq. (14.5), valid at thermal equilibrium. Adding a large number of one type of carrier forces the other type below n_i, so doping one type indirectly reduces the other.

front: Energy gaps of the group IV elements
back: (E_g)_C = 5.4 eV (insulator), (E_g)_Si = 1.1 eV, (E_g)_Ge = 0.72 eV and (E_g)_Sn = 0 (metal-like). The gap shrinks down the group, so the conductivity grows.

front: p-n junction formation: diffusion and drift
back: Holes diffuse p to n and electrons n to p along the concentration gradient (diffusion current). The uncovered ionised acceptors (negative, p-side) and donors (positive, n-side) create the field, which drives a drift current the other way. Equilibrium is reached when diffusion equals drift and the net current is zero.

The two space-charge layers together, about one-tenth of a micrometre thick, depleted of free charges. It has far higher resistance than the p- and n-regions, so an applied voltage drops almost entirely across it.
The potential difference across the unbiased junction, with the n-side positive relative to the p-side. It opposes further flow of carriers, preventing electrons from moving n to p at equilibrium.

p-side to the positive terminal, n-side to the negative terminal. The applied voltage opposes V_0, so the depletion layer narrows and the barrier falls to V_0 - V. Carriers cross and are injected as minority carriers (minority carrier injection), giving a current of the order of mA.

n-side positive, p-side negative. The applied voltage adds to V_0, so the barrier rises to V_0 + V and the depletion layer widens; diffusion current almost vanishes. The small drift current of minority carriers (a few microamperes) is the reverse saturation current, almost independent of voltage up to the breakdown voltage V_br.

Forward: current negligible until the cut-in (threshold) voltage, then rises almost exponentially - about 0.7 V for Si and 0.2 V for Ge. Reverse: a nearly constant saturation current of a few microamperes until breakdown, where the current rises sharply.
r_d = Delta V / Delta I  ... Eq. (14.6), the reciprocal of the slope of the V-I curve. Example 14.4 gives about 10 ohm in forward bias against 1.0 x 10^7 ohm in reverse bias for a silicon diode.

A diode conducts only when forward biased, so an alternating voltage produces current in one direction only. A circuit that does this is a rectifier. Half-wave: one diode, output only in alternate half cycles, output frequency = input frequency.

Two diodes whose p-sides go to the two ends of the secondary and whose n-sides are joined; the output is taken between that common point and the centre tap. D1 conducts in one half cycle, D2 in the other, so the load gets a pulse in every half cycle. A bridge version needs four diodes and no centre tap.
Half-wave: one pulse per input cycle, so f_out = f_in (50 Hz in gives 50 Hz out). Full-wave: two pulses per cycle, so f_out = 2 f_in (50 Hz in gives 100 Hz out).

A capacitor across the load charges to the peak of each rectified pulse and discharges through R_L between pulses. The fall is set by the time constant C R_L, so a large capacitance keeps the output nearly steady and close to the peak voltage; an inductor in series with the load works too.
